item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Thomas Markle was placed under house detention at his assisted living facility in Florida last weekByNardine Saad and Regan Morris, Los AngelesPublished10 November 2026, 20:02 GMTUpdated 6 minutes ago
Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, is back in federal custody in Florida after allegedly removing his ankle monitor, according to court documents.
Markle appeared before a federal magistrate judge in the Florida city of Tampa on Tuesday and was denied bond. Prosecutors say he removed the monitor early that morning.
US Judge Lindsay S Griffin found on Tuesday that Markle had violated the conditions of his pretrial release, court documents show.
Markle, who has denied possessing images of child sex abuse, was arrested in Florida last week and placed under house detention. He was also ordered to wear a location monitoring device.
The BBC has contacted his representatives.
Griffin described Markle's housing situation as "untenable", writing in the order revoking his pretrial release that "based on the lack of suitable housing, no condition or combination of conditions would reasonably assure the safety of any other person or the community and the defendant's appearance in court".
He also ordered a medical evaluation for Markle and said he "must receive all necessary and prescribed medication unless discontinued by a physician".
"Release conditions are court orders, not suggestions," Bill Essayli, the US attorney for Central California, wrote on X on Tuesday.
"We will continue to prosecute this case to the fullest extent of the law," he added.
Markle, 82, was first arrested last week after the FBI, acting on warrants, searched storage units in Los Angeles registered to him which he had rented since 2008, with the last payment being made in October this year, the DoJ said.

SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- The president of the Dominican Republic said Tuesday that his government is collaborating with El Salvador’s president and providing him with logistics and intelligence as some 2,500 troops from the Central American country battle violent gangs in Haiti.
Dominican President Luis Abinader spoke as the operations of the recently deployed Salvadoran troops to Haiti draw scrutiny because they are largely operating outside the framework of a U.N.-backed, multinational gang suppression force.

A new Gallup poll has found that support for the death penalty in the United States has fallen below 50 percent, marking the first time that the controversial practice has lost majority support since 1971.
The poll released on Tuesday found that 49 percent of people said they are in favour of capital punishment for those convicted of murder, the lowest level since 1966, while 45 percent say they are opposed.

“While statistically similar to last year’s 52 percent, the latest update marks the first time support has been below the majority level since 1971, when it was also at 49 percent,” Gallup said in a statement.
Support for the death penalty has been declining for decades amid concerns about issues of fairness, racial bias, high costs, botched executions and the possibility of innocent people being put to death. Decades of scholarship have also cast doubt on the argument that capital punishment deters crime.
Age, party divide

item.title: [CBS News World] 3 Iran-backed operatives indicted for alleged role in terror plots
item.description:
Three Iran-backed operatives have been charged with plotting a terrorist attack at a British Royal Air Force base in the United Kingdom where U.S. troops are stationed, the Justice Department announced on Tuesday.
Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood Al-Saadi was indicted in May on federal charges of conspiracy to provide material support to Iran-backed terrorist organizations, including Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Kata'ib Hizballah. He is accused in an eight-count superseding indictment made public Tuesday of attempting to coordinate with two other operatives to attack the British Royal Air Force base in the U.K. in September.
Al-Saadi is currently in federal custody in New York. In Tuesday's filing, the Justice Department alleged that he had plotted the air base attack with Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national, and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, by "passing them coded messages through third parties."
Mohajeri and al-Hassani are not in custody, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.
Federal prosecutors allege that beginning in August, Al-Saadi "directed and paid" associates in the United Kingdom to prepare for and arrange an attack at RAF Fairford, including directing an unnamed individual to conduct surveillance at the air base. Al-Saadi then allegedly later paid multiple unnamed people to organize vans and barrels of fuel, and to research chemical accelerants and buy metal to be used as shrapnel for a potential attack.
The indictment alleges that three individuals would then drive the vans, filled with fuel, to RAF Fairford, where they would explode.
Prosecutors say Al-Saadi told the individuals to mark the vans with custom decals to disguise themselves as a fuel delivery or pool supply business and directed his family members to pass messages to his co-conspirators.

item.title: [ABC News World] 4 grizzly bears linked by DNA to deadly attack on mother and daughter in Canada
item.description:
4 grizzly bears linked by DNA to deadly attack on mother and daughter in Canada
Canadian wildlife officials say four grizzly bears captured in western Canada were responsible for killing a mother and her adult daughter earlier this month in what investigators believe was a rare predatory attackByThe Associated PressNovember 10, 2026, 4:01 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
VANCOUVER, British Columbia -- Four grizzly bears captured in western Canada were responsible for killing a mother and her adult daughter this month in what investigators believe was a rare predatory attack, wildlife officials said Tuesday.
DNA tests conclusively linked a female grizzly and her three yearling cubs to the deaths of Jenny Balcarras, 48, and her 20-year-old daughter, Selah Reed, the British Columbia Conservation Officer Service said. All four bears were killed to protect the public.
“Our investigation also found that this attack likely involved predatory behavior, which I can tell you is very rare,” Inspector Jeff Tyre told an online briefing.
“That is to say, we don’t know how it started, but we know how it ended.”
The women’s remains were found about 150 meters (490 feet) apart near a trail outside Bella Coola, a remote community about 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) north of Vancouver.
Family members raised the alarm after Reed missed a routine Saturday night call with her sister. Searchers found her mother’s remains first, then discovered Reed’s remains in a bear cache, where bears store food.
Tyre said the bears were not involved in a separate grizzly attack last November on a group of about 20 elementary school students and teachers in the same area. Eleven people were injured, including two critically.

item.description:
Street boxing matches gain popularity in Bogota
Santiago Abril has been organizing pop-up boxing matches in parks around Bogota, Colombia, without official permitsByASTRID SUÁREZ Associated Press and MARKO ÁLVAREZ Associated PressNovember 10, 2026, 2:32 PM
BOGOTA, Colombia -- In a park on the outskirts of Colombia’s capital, Santiago Abril set up a mat made with interlocking rubber panels and assembled an octagonal structure resembling a mixed martial arts cage.
The portable ring, made of rubber and plastic, serves as the stage for the improvised boxing matches that Abril has organized for months at parks in Bogota, mostly without official permits.
Dozens of young men and women gather on weekends for Abril’s pop-up fights, where strangers face off without the lengthy preparations required for regular boxing matches. Some want to test their boxing skills. Others are looking for a new thrill.
Women pay around $5 to compete, while men pay $15. Organizers provide boxing gloves but no headgear. Cash prizes of around $100 are given to those who can win two or three fights in a row in hastily organized tournaments.
For Ingrid Prieto, a 29-year-old who recently participated in a fight, boxing is a form of therapy.
“When I was young, I used to get in a lot of fights, so I began to practice taekwondo,” she said, adding that contact sports have helped her to channel her emotions.
Eliber Parra García, 27, repairs mobile phones for a living. He said he joined the pop-up fights to experience what it feels like to be a professional boxer, and also for the adrenaline that comes with fighting and the chance to make some money. “I have an orange belt in judo,” Parra García said. “But I know very little about boxing.”
Bogota’s municipal government told the Associated Press that the fights require permits and a plan for dealing with emergencies that must be submitted to authorities.

item.title: [CBS News World] Jockey Izzy Neale, 22, dies after her horse falls during race
item.description:
Jockey Izzy Neale died on Tuesday, two days after her horse fell during a race in Australia, the Racing NSW state thoroughbred authority said.
The 22-year-old Neale suffered injuries Sunday when her horse Marnoo fell and suffered a fatal leg injury in the homestretch of a 1-mile race at Warren racecourse.
She was unconscious when airlifted to a hospital, and Racing NSW released a statement Tuesday from her family that she had died.
"Izzy rode horses before she could walk. Her love of horses was a lifelong passion that, more recently, had grown into a love of racing," the statement said of Neale, who rode 88 winners in her career.
Izzy Neale gives a thumbs-up after winning at Rosehill Gardens on July 4, 2026, in Sydney, Australia.
Jeremy Ng/Getty Images
"Through organ donation, Izzy will give others the chance of life, bringing some comfort to our family amid this devastating loss."
Rider Diego Montes de Oca was also dislodged from his horse during the race, Racing NSW said in a statement, adding that he suffered a foot injury but was later discharged from the hospital.
Neale had 699 career starts in her career, local media reported.
Her brother Tommy Neale wrote on Facebook that he couldn't "believe what's happened," adding: "You'll always be my lil baby sister, you were my best friend an we always was so close so I dunno how I'm gonna deal with this."
Izzy Neale smiles after winning at Rosehill Gardens on July 4, 2026, in Sydney, Australia.

item.description:
Image source, EPAImage caption,
Najib smiles to reporters at the Kuala Lumpur High Court after it cleared the way for him to go homeBySimon FraserAsia digital editor, LondonPublished3 hours ago
Malaysia's disgraced former Prime Minister Najib Razak has arrived home to begin serving the rest of a jail sentence for corruption under house arrest.
There was a big media presence at his Kuala Lumpur residence to see the 73-year-old return from prison in an SUV late on Tuesday night, escorted by a heavily armed police convoy.
Najib's return ended a four-year prison stint after he was found guilty over the embezzlement of billions of dollars from the country's sovereign wealth fund.
The 1MDB scandal brought down his government and made headlines around the world when it came to light a decade ago, embroiling prominent figures from Malaysia to Goldman Sachs and Hollywood.
Investigators estimated that $4.5bn (£3.3bn) was siphoned from the state-owned wealth fund, which Najib co-founded, into private pockets, including his own. More than $1bn allegedly ended up in accounts linked to Najib, according to prosecutors.
Najib's lawyers claim he had been misled by his advisers - in particular the financier Jho Low, who has maintained his innocence and remains at large.
Image source, ReutersImage caption,
Journalists jostled for a glimpse of Najib as he was driven to his home, which has been declared a federal prison
Najib's mansion in one of the capital's most exclusive neighbourhoods was declared a federal prison ahead of his homecoming on Tuesday.
Critics said his release from jail undermined efforts to fight corruption and questioned its legal basis, saying Malaysian law made no provision for house arrest.
Najib, who was prime minister from 2009 to 2018, denied wrongdoing but was convicted at two separate trials.
In the first trial he was sentenced in 2020 to 12 years in prison and jailed in 2022. The term was later halved on appeal.

Gadi Eisenkot has vowed to oust Benjamin Netanyahu, but still has to get enough parties on boardByRaffi BergPublished10 November 2026, 12:25 GMTUpdated 5 hours ago
Israel's new parliament has been sworn in, as opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot seeks to oust caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The former army chief has been tasked with forming a government after receiving more recommendations from members of the Knesset than Netanyahu, although not all those backing him are willing to govern together.
Eisenkot's bloc of four parties won 48 seats in October's election, while Netanyahu's bloc won 53, leaving both short of a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. He has 28 days to build a coalition, with a possible two-week extension.
Almost half of the new MKs did not serve in the previous parliament, while Arab-led parties have a record number of seats.
Shortly after they were sworn in, Netanyahu and Eisenkot warned parliament about the perils of supporting a government led by the other.
"[And] to those who are thinking of establishing a government that includes supporters of terror and haters of Israel, or that will be dependent on them, I ask you, are you prepared to be dependent on those whose goal is the destruction of the Jewish state?" said Netanyahu, alluding to the prospect of an Eisenkot-led government reliant on support from Arab parties.
He also appealed for the formation of a government of national unity as the only way to confront what he said was the threat of "a nuclear Iran".
Eisenkot sharply criticised Netanyahu's comments.
"I sat and listened to the outgoing prime minister's delusional, divisive, hate-filled and shameful speech, exploiting a state occasion," he said. "I am now even more convinced that he is unfit to remain in office for even one more minute."

People could start taking trips in so-called flying cars in China as soon as next summer, the manufacturer of a two-seater vehicle with autopilot model has said.
Deli Zhao, the chief executive of the Chinese flying car company XPeng, said the $300,000 (£225,000) low-altitude device would be ready for use by recreational users in rural locations and by emergency services in the second half of 2027. After 10 years of development including trials of flying motorbikes at the company’s Guangzhou base, it has been approved by China’s civil aviation authorities for limited use.
The small cockpit is about the size of a Fiat 500 car and the vehicle is lifted into the air by six drone-like battery-powered propellers and steered by a simple joystick. It can also fly autonomously to a programmed destination, but Xhao, a trained pilot, claimed he could teach anyone to fly it in five minutes.
The price tag for the contraption includes a six-wheel van about the size of a Ford Transit, out of the back of which the flying vehicle unfolds “just like the Transformers”, said Zhao. He has been developing flying cars for almost a decade and said he was part-inspired by the flying creatures ridden by humans in the Harry Potter stories and the Green Goblin’s flying skateboard from the Spider-Man comics.

A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.

US and rest of world must follow China’s lead on green energy, says John Kerry
Former US secretary of state says most nations are ‘stumbling along’ while Beijing has ‘hugely accelerated’
Cop31 live – latest updates
China is leading the world in moving away from fossil fuels, and the rest of the globe – including the US – must now follow, the former US secretary of state John Kerry has told the Guardian, as Cop watchers wonder exactly how China is going to approach this year’s climate summit.
As Cop31 opens – this year the climate conference is in Turkey – there is plenty of speculation about whether China will finally step into the leadership role that it has long avoided. In its latest “five-year plan” adopted in March 2026, China for the first time pledged to “actively participate in and lead global climate governance”. Cop31 could provide the first indications Beijing is ready to put that rhetoric into action, something it has historically been reluctant to do.
Green energy is a vital component of the export engine that has kept China’s sluggish post-pandemic economy on track. The success of its exports stands in contrast to its failure to significantly boost domestic general consumption, a structural weakness that has persistently vexed leaders.
In 2025, clean-tech exports surpassed $220bn, and they should grow again this year; the world’s largest emitter is now the world’s leading supplier of clean energy technology. No more getting away with it … Traces of Justice. Photograph: Trinity/CineAsia
View image in fullscreen
No more getting away with it … Traces of Justice. Photograph: Trinity/CineAsiaReview
Traces of Justice review – ‘Chinese Sherlock Holmes’ at centre of arresting forensic cop thriller
Based on real scientist Cui Daozhi, this sharp feature has thumping set pieces and knotty puzzles set across 30 years of gripping cases
The latest from Chen Sicheng, prime mover behind the hit Detective Chinatown franchise, offers a disarming mix of propaganda, copaganda and gripping narrative. It’s essentially a portmanteau biopic: its hero is Cui Xun, a fictional stand-in for the venerable Cui Daozhi, a still-extant real-life figure who so revolutionised forensic science he became known as “China’s Sherlock Holmes”. Ripping three-and-a-bit tales from the casebook – involving a 1970s child killer, a grisly 1980s multiple murder and a 1990s bus bombing (plus one lingering loose end), Chen constructs a history of forensic investigation that is also, in variably oblique ways, a history of Chinese law enforcement, which is shown evolving from boozy, gloveless crime-scene trampling to something far more streamlined and professional.
Within the handsome period framework, Chen follows the science: one era’s crazy innovation becomes commonplace in the next. A rookie Cui (played here by Zhang Yi, ageing up subtly) uses boiled potatoes to take dental imprints; when these run out, he and his colleagues start biting one another’s cheeks to make their points. (Their scars are a terrific visual gag: scientists literally showing their working.) By the 90s, when Cui is heading a team working out of a vast, well-staffed warehouse, we seem mere moments away from David Caruso’s sunglasses and memorable Who guitar riffs. Hundreds of billions of dollars have been wiped off the value of Nvidia after the US chipmaker announced an independent investigation would be carried out into its chief executive's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
The tech firm saw its shares fall by about 4% by close of trade on Monday after Jensen Huang admitted having an extramarital affair.
Nvidia's probe came after reports that the US believed the Nvidia boss had been targeted in an espionage campaign by China.
However, China has rejected the claims, with its foreign ministry saying allegations about Chinese spies were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".
Nvidia said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, but a statement by the firm's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and chief executive Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort".
US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report, external.
The report said Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.
Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.
Jensen Huang admitted he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. He added he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation.

People at the scene of the collision in Giza province. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images
Collision of two trains in Egypt kills at least seven
President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 50km from Cairo
Seven people were killed and at least 125 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said.
The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 50km (30 miles) south of Cairo, when a train travelling to Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry.
An inspection indicated that the Cairo-Aswan train had been stationary on the same track, officials said.
The health ministry gave the casualty toll, adding more than 70 of the injured were discharged after receiving treatment.
Train derailments and crashes are common in Egypt, where the railway system has a history of mismanagement and poor maintenance of equipment. In recent years the government has announced modernisation initiatives to improve its railways.
Ayman Gamal, a resident of Kafr Girza in al-Ayyat where the crash occurred, said people rushed to the scene, pulled out survivors and called ambulances.
Gamal said he saw about 80 of the injured being taken by ambulances to hospital. Some passengers were trapped inside one of the carriages of the stationary train and died, he said.
View image in fullscreen
People search for survivors after the collision. Photograph: AP
Egypt’s president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said in a social media post that he had ordered a prompt investigation.

How African philosophies inspired a new approach to staging film festivals in Manchester
See My World, an event highlighting the pan-African thought via film, poetry and dance, builds on momentum sparked by local activists and creatives
African philosophies including exploring how lessons from the past can shape the present and near future have inspired a film festival coming to Manchester.
See My World, a day dedicated to independent creators from across the African diaspora in the north of England, will take place at the Contact theatre on 21 November.
The festival is part of See My World’s year-round programme showcasing pan-African arts, culture and events.
It reflects the determination among creatives and activists in Manchester to build on the legacy of the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester – which connected luminaries of postwar independence movements with a shared vision of liberation – after last year’s 80th anniversary commemorations.
See My World’s CEO and artistic director, Tunde Adekoya, said this month’s film festival was taking inspiration from across the spectrum of pan-African thought, including the works of Kenyan writers John Mbiti, an Anglican theologian who died in 2019, and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, the author of the groundbreaking 1986 book Decolonising the Mind who died last year.
Both writers rejected the colonial conceit that African thought was inferior, stressed the importance of community and saw reclaiming African ways of knowing as essential to a people’s self-understanding.
